citation: docs/architecture.md, agent states; herdr's five states observed in docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 3
why: Agent states are the reason this project exists, so reading one wrongly is not a display bug. Five states, not four: `unknown` is a state an agent can genuinely be in - a pane whose harness we cannot classify - and it renders as itself. The names are listed one per case rather than looped over, so that the set is pinned as data: a language that spelled one of them differently would otherwise pass a round-trip test while disagreeing with the daemon.

cases.name: working
cases.why: The state an agent spends most of its time in, and the one whose absence would make a busy pane look idle.

cases.name: blocked
cases.why: The state attention routing exists for: an agent that needs a person. Misreading it as idle is the failure that makes the whole feature pointless.

cases.name: idle
cases.why: Nothing running. Distinct from done, which herdr derives as idle-on-an-unseen-pane rather than storing.

cases.name: done
cases.why: Never stored by a backend - it is idle on a pane nobody has seen. Muster reads the derived value rather than computing it, so the name still has to survive the wire.

cases.name: unknown
cases.why: A state in its own right, not an error. An agent we failed to read is not an agent that finished.

cases.name: a state we have never heard of fails closed onto unknown
cases.why: herdr's API is explicitly unstable and ships weekly, so a state we have never heard of is a thing it may add next week. Failing closed shows an honest 'we don't know' instead of crashing or - far worse - quietly reading a novel state as idle and telling the user nothing needs them.

cases.name: an empty state reads as unknown
cases.why: The shape a missing field takes after a permissive decode. Same reasoning as an unrecognized name, reached by the more likely route.
